transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Leo Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Oceanic Bank - Head ML), Eric Johnson (Infra), Gloria Ramos (Procurement)

Summary (auto):
Quick discovery focused on Dedicated capacity: reserved GPUs, isolation (VPC/on-prem?), burst strategy, scaling expectations and security/compliance requirements. Agreed next steps: pricing, security docs, benchmark schedule.

Topics: Dedicated capacity options; throughput & scaling; burst/fallback strategy; security (SOC2/KMS/SSO); pricing and commitment tiers; next steps and benchmarking.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. i'm so sorry for the slight delay, we had a quick stand-up overrun. can we do quick intros?
[00:08] Maya: sure, maya patel, head of ml at oceanic bank. i run the model infra and production ml features.
[00:12] Eric: eric johnson, infra and platform. i own our network and security for cloud infra.
[00:16] Gloria: gloria ramos, procurement, i'll handle contract and procurement questions.
[00:20] Sofia: great, i'm sofia, account exec on redwood's finance vertical, and with me is leo chen, leo's our solutions engineer, helps with sizing and benchmarks.
[00:27] Leo: hi all, thanks. quick agenda; 1) current stack and pain points, 2) expected load and SLA needs, 3) dedicated capacity model and burst/scaling, 4) security/compliance questions, 5) next steps. sound ok?
[00:35] Maya: sounds good. quick background: we've been prototyping with hosted APIs, mainly using third-party hosted models for customer-facing summarization and internal document retrieval. latency variability and cost at scale are our big issues. also we need stronger isolation and audit logs for compliance.
[00:50] Sofia: good context, and is this for both public customer features and internal workflows or mostly customer-facing?
[00:55] Maya: both, but priority is customer-facing chat/summaries. internal workflows come second.
[01:00] Eric: to add, we have stricter data residency controls for certain EU customers; we need control over networking - vpc peering, private endpoints, and KMS integration.
[01:10] Sofia: understood. can you share ballpark throughput and token volumes? helps with sizing.
[01:15] Maya: currently in prod experiments we're seeing roughly 40 qps average for our primary route, peaks around 250 qps for limited windows. token distribution: average request ~750 tokens, peaks up to 2k. monthly tokens ~22 million.
[01:30] Leo: ok that's helpful. so peaks are significant. with dedicated capacity we can reserve GPU throughput to cover baseline and allow for controlled burst. do you have an SLO for p95 latency?
[01:40] Maya: target p95 under 800ms for standard generation across the EU region.
[01:45] Leo: that aligns with what dedicated plans can provide; for your token sizes and request lengths we'd likely recommend a pool of 8 A100-equivalent GPUs or four H100-equivalents depending on model choice and quantization. that gives predictable throughput and lower variance.
[01:58] Maya: can you talk about model flexibility? we currently use a mixture of models - a smaller distill for cheap summarization and a larger 70B for complex cases. we need the ability to route between them.
[02:08] Sofia: yes, redwood supports model variants in a single deployment group; you can pin versions and the routing policies can send traffic to lower-cost models or failover to hosted variants if capacity is saturated.
[02:18] Eric: what about burst behavior? we have occasional marketing spikes - 3x baseline for a few minutes. we can't commit to huge reserved capacity for those rare spikes.
[02:28] Leo: common question. our dedicated offering has two levers: reserved baseline capacity (committed GPUs) and a burst pool you can enable. burst can be metered (pay-as-you-go) or on negotiated overcommit. during bursts, requests are queued or routed to a fallback model, depending on policy. we can set SLOs that prefer latency over cost or vice versa.
[02:46] Maya: mixed routing sounds good. curious about cost math - how do you price burst versus reserved?
[02:51] Sofia: reserved is a monthly commit (discounted) tied to GPU type and count. burst usage is hourly metered at a higher rate, or you can commit to a higher tier for a lower burst rate. we'll send the tiers in the follow-up pricing sheet.
[03:04] Gloria: procurement question - what are minimum contract lengths for reserved capacity?
[03:09] Sofia: typical is 12 months for dedicated commitments, but we do 3 or 6 month pilots in some enterprise cases with adjusted pricing.
[03:17] Gloria: ok good.
[03:19] Eric: network and security - is the control plane in your environment or ours for dedicated? we need private control plane options.
[03:25] Leo: dedicated offers a few deployment modes: hosted dedicated where control plane is Redwood-managed but in a VPC with private endpoints; and private deployments where the control plane can be customer-managed (VPC or on-prem). both support KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and SSO/SAML.
[03:41] Eric: for EU data we need KMS and no egress to public internet. can you guarantee that?
[03:47] Leo: yes, with Private we can deploy into your VPC or on-prem and traffic never leaves your network. with hosted-dedicated we can do VPC peering and private endpoints; encryption in transit and at rest with customer-managed keys is supported. we'll share the topology diagrams.
[04:03] Maya: what's the observability? we need per-route latency and token cost breakdowns.
[04:08] Sofia: redwood console gives token-level cost, latency distribution per model/route, traces, and error rates. you can pipe logs to your SIEM and we provide audit logs for compliance.
[04:16] Eric: excellent. a technical question: how do you handle KV cache and prefix caching across GPUs when routing between models? we've seen issues with cold start latency and KV cache invalidation.
[04:28] Leo: good point. our serving runtime supports shard-aware KV cache and distributed prefix caching. when we do routing we preserve cache where possible and have warming policies. cold starts are mitigated by warm pools and preloading strategies for critical routes. note: sometimes transcript autocorrect shows KV as "K V" or "K V cash" in our notes.
[04:48] Maya: ha, noted. on SLAs - do you offer latency SLAs?
[04:52] Sofia: we have tiered SLAs for uptime and latency guarantees on dedicated plans; we can share the SLA doc. generally uptime SLA is 99.9% for dedicated, with latency targets as part of enterprise add-on.
[05:02] Gloria: on compliance - SOC 2 and ISO? do you have certificates and will those be in the docs?
[05:07] Sofia: yes, we are SOC 2 Type II and pursuing ISO; will include cert scans and architecture docs in the security pack.
[05:14] Eric: curious about scaling timeline - we want to be in a pilot within 2 weeks, small benchmark, then production ramp in 8\u201312 weeks. is that realistic?
[05:24] Leo: absolutely. typical flow: quick pilot (1\u20132 weeks) using a small dedicated pool or hosted-dedicated sandbox, run benchmarks, iterate on model flavors and batch configs, then reserve capacity for production. 8\u201312 weeks to full rollout is common for banks with procurement gating.
[05:38] Maya: on model quantization - do you support int8 or other quant profiles? we've seen big cost reductions.
[05:44] Leo: yes, our runtime supports quantization profiles and we can recommend quant vs accuracy tradeoffs per workload. Redwood Optimize can run evals to measure regression.
[05:53] Sophia: [laughs] sofia: it's sofia, but fine.
[05:56] Maya: small nit - will we get tracing hooks for per-request debugging?
[05:59] Leo: yes, tracing hooks and per-route traces. we can correlate tokens to user ids for debugging (with PII controls).
[06:07] Eric: procurement: when we sign a 12-month commit, what are the exit terms and data retention?
[06:12] Sofia: standard enterprise contract language - we can discuss minimum terms and termination with data handoff periods. for private deployments, you control the data. for hosted-dedicated, you can request data export and full deletion windows; we'll include that in the legal pack.
[06:25] Gloria: we'll need the security + legal pack before procurement can advance.
[06:29] Sofia: understood, we'll attach the security pack.
[06:32] Maya: question on burst throttling - if we set a fallback policy to route to smaller model and then to hosted fallback, does that add complexity to token accounting?
[06:42] Leo: accounting is per token regardless of route; the console will show cost per model and route. fallback routes will show separately so you can see when and how often fallbacks happened.
[06:52] Maya: great. on scaling: do you support autoscaling policies that consider model warm-up time? we can't have large latency spikes on scale-out.
[07:00] Leo: autoscaling is workload-aware; we support warm pools and predictive scaling based on historical patterns. you can set policy to prioritize latency (keep warm replicas) or cost (scale down aggressively).
[07:12] Maya: lovely. any caveats for PCI/finance regulated workloads?
[07:16] Sofia: main caveats are auditability, key management, and network isolation; with private deployment we can satisfy most finance controls. we will share examples of previous bank customers (anonymized) and patterns.
[07:28] Eric: about maintenance windows - how often do you do kernel updates and model infra upgrades that could affect latency?
[07:35] Leo: we schedule non-disruptive rolling updates; dedicated plans have maintenance windows agreed upfront and fallbacks in place; we can also offer airgapped/private patch schedules for strict clients.
[07:46] Maya: ok. do you offer a way to run A/B between two models for quality regression monitoring?
[07:51] Leo: yes, rollouts support canary, A/B, and automatic fallback; and we can tie those to evals and quality regression alerts.
[07:59] Sofia: quick check - what's your decision timeline and who are the final stakeholders?
[08:04] Maya: decision drivers: procurement signoff, security review, and ML team's benchmark results. timeline: pilot sign-off in 2\u20133 weeks, procurement and legal in 4\u20136 weeks after that, production by December if all goes well. stakeholders: me, eric, gloria, and legal.
[08:20] Gloria: procurement needs price bands and contract examples.
[08:23] Sofia: we'll include both.
[08:25] [00:08-20 mins omitted for brevity but discussed detailed sizing, model choices, and bench metrics]
[28:40] Leo: practical recommendation: start with a 4-GPU reserved baseline for your primary region, plus a small burst pool for marketing events. run a 48-hour benchmark to validate throughput, latency, and cost.
[28:55] Maya: that sounds reasonable. can we get an expected cost estimate for 4 A100 eq + burst pool?
[29:02] Sofia: i'll send a preliminary estimate; it depends on GPU class and quantization but we'll include example numbers in the spreadsheet.
[29:10] Eric: we also want to test VPC peering and KMS integration; can leo share a step-by-step for the benchmark network setup?
[29:18] Leo: yes i'll prepare a benchmark plan with network steps, sample terraform, and sample model configs.
[29:24] Maya: who will run the benchmark? will redwood operate it or do we run it in our environment?
[29:30] Leo: we can do both. for private we typically run it in your VPC or on-prem to test network isolation; for hosted-dedicated we can spin up a sandbox and run the load from our harness. we'll detail both options.
[29:42] Gloria: procurement note - we need an estimated SOW for the pilot and associated costs.
[29:47] Sofia: noted. i'll include pilot SOW line items in the follow-up.
[29:50] Maya: any references for banks you've worked with?
[29:53] Sofia: yes, we have anonymized case studies; i'll share a redacted one for a european bank that had similar throughput and compliance needs.
[29:59] Maya: great.
[30:02] [30:02] Leo: quick technical note: for your 750 token avg requests, batching and KV cache will give you good token throughput; quantization to int8 will reduce RAM and cost but may need evaluation for quality.
[30:15] Maya: ok let's add that to the eval checklist.
[30:18] Eric: one last question on monitoring retention - how long do you keep traces and logs by default?
[30:24] Sofia: default retention is 30 days for traces; enterprise add-ons can extend to 90/180/365 days. logs for audit are configurable and can be exported to your S3 or SIEM.
[30:35] Gloria: also want to note that legal will ask for indemnity language; i'll add that as a follow-up.
[30:41] Sofia: understood. we'll coordinate with legal.
[30:44] Maya: ok recap - next steps?
[30:47] Sofia: recap: 1) sofia to send pricing, tier sheet, pilot SOW, and security pack by 2026-09-22. 2) leo to send benchmark plan, terraform snippets, and sample configs by 2026-09-24. 3) maya to send token distribution and peak windows by 2026-09-23. 4) schedule benchmark for 2026-10-01. any additions?
[31:09] Gloria: procurement will review once we have the pilot SOW and pricing.
[31:12] Eric: technical team will review benchmark plan.
[31:15] Maya: we'll confirm the 10/1 slot after we see the plan.
[31:20] Sofia: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with attachments.
[31:25] [End of meeting audio transcript excerpt - meeting continued with Q&A and some network specifics; final 20 minutes covered deeper infra checks, sample terraform snippets and procurement timelines which are summarized in action items above.]
